utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. There are certain technical difficulties facing us this afternoon, but the proceedings can be recorded. The exhibits to be used by the Defence are in hard copy, the ELMO will work, and you will see it on the screen, and we now already have at least part of the system working. There's a transcript before me, although even if that disappears we can still carry on because it will be compiled at a later stage. So let's have the witness back, please. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination by Mr. Cepic will continue in a moment. As I'm sure you are very well aware, the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today until it is completed. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We talked about two locations yesterday, Mali Alas and Slovinje. Then we saw a request for an investigation concerning Slovinje. What I want to know is this: Initially who were charges brought against in relation to these two locations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to one of these, I told you yesterday what I knew and I saw that document about Slovinje --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm asking you initially, as soon as it was learned.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the event became known, no charges were pressed against anyone because in order to instigate proceedings one must first identify a potential perpetrator. However, you can start proceedings against unknown perpetrators or unidentified perpetrators. There is an investigating judge who carries out an investigation to see if it is possible to track down a perpetrator and in order to gather evidence that may later be used for the purposes of a trial. So this is the essence of the investigations that we carried out at the time. If I may, as for Mali Alas, I know we launched an investigation while we were still in Pristina and then the investigating judge submitted a document about that to the military prosecutor of the corps, and then he requested further action about this. And then when we came to Nis, the military court there, I know for sure that somewhere in Serbia, in Sombor or in Apatin, there were the investigating judges of the military court in Nis together with the military prosecutor, they went there to interview or question a number of reservists, reserve soldiers, who had been in the area. I think the document is now somewhere in the war crimes section of the Belgrade Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, why was this document forwarded to a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The case file was forwarded to a civilian court because after the military prosecutor had done everything that he was supposed to do the case file was forwarded to a prosecutor and then he concluded, based on everything that had been gathered, that no military personnel were involved. And then he decided to declare himself as having no jurisdiction over the matter and then he forwarded the case file to the district prosecutor in Pristina. Of course that prosecutor's office was then moved to another town or city, I'm not sure which one, but somewhere in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember what the situation was in relation to this other case, Slovinje?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the prosecutor went forward in a similar manner and established eventually that no military personnel had been involved. We saw that request for investigation yesterday. There was some other persons who were suspected of having committed this crime, not military personnel, but rather civilians from that area. "Suspicion," I say. I'm not sure if it was them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please place this document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the last part of Mr. Cepic's remark. Could Mr. Cepic please be asked to move closer to his microphone or to speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the end of your question there --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Was missed by the interpreter. After you identified the document to the usher, what else did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for 5D1343 to be placed on the ELMO for technical reasons, for reasons of the technical insufficiencies that we are facing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, this is a letter of our government to the OTP. There is reference here to criminal proceedings against Dragoljub Cirkovic. Are you familiar with this case, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I am because I handled this case after an indictment had been issued against Mr. Cirkovic for murder, which is exactly what we see here. Once the war had been over, he was no longer a military official and the military court in Nis, no longer had jurisdiction over the case. Then the matter was forwarded to another court - I'm not sure which one - I think Pec, a civilian court that would have had jurisdiction over the matter. And you can tell by looking at this that he was convicted, he got a prison sentence, and there is an appeal that is underway, and the Supreme Court is now handling this appeal. Let me tell you something else. Cirkovic and a great number of other people were on remand in Lipljan. He was then taking to Nis, and from there, onwards, he had been escorted to the Nis prison first and then he was taken from there to this court which happened to have jurisdiction over the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many persons were sentenced to -- how many persons were detained during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I carried out my own analysis, and then after the war I continued my work with the military court and we had over 300 persons who were on remand during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In June 1999 there was the withdrawal from Kosovo and Metohija. After that what was done with these persons who were on remand?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Kumanovo Agreement we were told to move these detainees to the correctional facility in Nis on the 9th and 10th of June. I can't remember specifically. Buses were sent for that purpose. And I remember that there were two buses that were used for this purpose and neither were full; therefore, a total of about 70 detainees who were transferred to Nis. The remaining persons were set free. We only transferred those who we believed it was necessary to keep in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After a state of war had been declared over or terminated - and you mentioned the example of Cirkovic a while ago, you say that this case was forwarded to a civilian court because this person was now no longer a military official, a member of the army - in terms of percentage, can you tell us how many other cases like that were referred to a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to talk about percentage, but I can tell you that based on the report it would seem that crimes such as this one, crimes of this nature, were mostly perpetrated by reservists. Once a state of war had been declared over, these persons were no longer military personnel. And then when we were dealing with crimes that were not within -- under the exclusive jurisdiction of military courts since these persons were no longer military personnel or members of the army, the military courts were no longer in charge of these cases. However, during the war, before these persons started being members of the army and the indictment had already taken effect, then it would have been a military court that had jurisdiction over the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit 5D1290. [In English] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there's something wrong with the last sentence of the last answer in English. It says: "However, during the war, before these persons started being members of the army and the indictment had already taken effect, then it would have been a military court that had jurisdiction ..." Should that not be after these people became members of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war they were no longer military men. That's what it should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However -- my apologies. But if it was before they stopped being military officials and the indictment had already taken effect, a military court would have had jurisdiction over the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The word in English is "started" and it should have been "stopped," so the position has been clarified. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, does this document on the ELMO seem familiar?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What's it about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a report on the work of the military court attached to the corps command which was sent periodically to the corps command in order to be passed down the chain of command to lower-ranking units so that the entire corps, to the extent possible, was familiarised with the work of the military court in order to know which crimes were prosecuted. Prevention was the principal objective of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, can you explain briefly Article 47, Article 165, Article 166?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this report, in addition to crimes there is this preceding portion against the Army of Yugoslavia, and then we state here that proceedings are underway before the military court for crimes under Article 47 of the Criminal Code of Serbia, this is murder, one officer, one NCO, 12 soldiers; and then theft, 26 soldiers; aggravated theft, 71; three officers, eight NCOs. These are proceedings that were underway before the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is this, 174? What crime is that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is when a vehicle is seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How many persons were prosecuted at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 56, that's what I see here. This is a crime against property.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what is the breakdown?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One officer, 52 NC -- 42 NCOs and one unknown perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for seized vehicles, in practical terms were there cases in which vehicles were seized?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what our law says. Any kind of material gain must be taken away that is acquired in this manner. We took those vehicles back and we had a special pound, parking lot, for these vehicles in Pristina that was secured by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about after the war, did you return vehicles to owners from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once it had been established who the owner of a vehicle was, it was the court's responsibility to do just that and it was only logical that the owner should get back as quick as possible what rightfully belonged to him. There was several such criminal cases where I returned vehicles like that. Once I returned a large truck. As soon as I had documents on my table about the truck's ownership, then I was adamant that the truck should be returned to its rightful owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, who did you report to? In addition to this report that you sent to the corps, did you report to anyone else about the work of the court?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis, to the section of the supreme military court that was based in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We're running out of time now and these are my last questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please, to pass these two documents to the witness. These are 5D1348 and 5D1349.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Mladenovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report by the section of the supreme military court in Nis. It was delivered to the army command, and it talks about what the military courts dealt with on the previous day, those that covered the area under the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is the number for this document? It's 5D13 -- in the top right corner, just for the sake of clarity, 1349. Thank you. Will you please look at the previous day. What were the steps taken by your court, according to this report, if you can find that for us, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here that the court that was attached to the command of the Pristina Corps carried out four on-site investigations. One person was detained and four requests were received to carry out investigation. Two persons were indicted, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the other document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is this about, this document, 5D1348?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's similar as the previous one, a report on the work of military courts from the territory under the 3rd Army for the 3rd and this is the report in relation to the 4th and this is about what they did on the 3rd, the previous day. And you can see if you look at this report specifically, specifically the command of the Pristina Corps, two were in custody, seven were detained, and nine were unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And this was about what day --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please be asked to speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- There's been an overlap between you. Could you be careful to avoid it and could you ask that question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, during what period of time -- to what period of time does a report pertain?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a period of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A general question. In accordance with our legislation at that time, back then as well as nowadays, when it comes to the statute of limitations, what is the statute of limitations for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has always been a principle that the statute of limitations does not run out when it comes to these kinds of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have just two or three more questions. Did any officer of the Army of Yugoslavia during the war address you with a request to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Cepic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you'll need to repeat that question. You're speaking away from the microphone and not everything is being picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, during the war did any officer of the Army of Yugoslavia ever address you with any type of a request to affect a court trial or proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war did you have any contact with the corps commander, General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards the military judiciary?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a very appropriate attitude, if I may say so, a very fair one. By your leave I can elaborate on this. But to put it briefly, quite a proper attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could I ask a question of the witness on that note. I'd like to find out what made you say that his attitude was an appropriate and proper one? Could I hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. When speaking of his proper attitude or an appropriate attitude, what I mean to say is that as a corps commander he ensured that during the war all resources were there that were required for a normal functioning of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, there were no attempts by any officer to affect or influence court proceedings, and I did not really have any other cooperation with the corps commander; I wasn't required to have any kind of cooperation. When it comes to the court established during the wartime, the task of the corps command was only to ensure logistics and that kind of a cooperation existed there. That's why I say that this transpired very properly because everything functioned. This was taking place during the war. Had it not been for the command and its efforts to ensure that we had all the resources there, I'm sure that it would have functioned much less efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My last question: Was the corps commander interested in learning whether people were prosecuted and whether work was undertaken in order to work on all of the cases and all of the criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. When it comes to cases from this field, when it comes to these proceedings, I can say that the corps commander perhaps sometimes overreacted in his requests to ensure that this was investigated properly from all angles. What I mean to say is that in a very proper manner he asked from me, as the president of the court, to ensure that an investigative judge was present during the sanitisation of the terrain. According to the Law on Criminal Procedure when it comes to sanitisation, it is not necessary that an investigative judge is present. It is strictly regulated which organs need to be present when that work is undertaken. It was my opinion that not only because the law stipulated so but also because we had already had some four or five cases where investigative judges could have come to serious harm, be it by sniper fire from armed groups of the KLA but also from the NATO aviation. And this was my guiding principle when I took a restrictive approach to investigative judges being sent there, because an investigative judge in our system is an officer in uniform. When sanitisation is carried out, a lot of other persons are present - forensic experts, pathologists, military security, and so on. All of them wear uniforms and all of them are targets. All of them are targets out there in the field. However, later on I realised that the fact that the commander insisted on them being present was actually very useful because the presence of an investigative judge in such cases carries more of a probative value later on in criminal proceedings once a perpetrator is discovered. On the other hand, this sanitisation of the terrain or battle-field doesn't mean any sweeping of the terrain; it's more of a sanitary measure, that is the nature of it, in order to prevent any infections emerging, any danger to the civilians. Because when a sanitisation is carried out certain sanitary measures are carried out, carcuses of animals are removed and so on. It is not anything that has to do with what other investigative judges ordered, to remove corpses and bodies of victims, no; quite the contrary, the purpose of this is to ensure that in the presence of an investigative judge all is properly documented and that these people are ensured a dignified burial and that their remains are turned over to their families. In this way we abided by a proper procedure, and when this was further prosecuted before the court in Nis, some 600 victims were identified and the circumstances of their death were as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, my name is Dan Ivetic, and as counsel for Sreten Lukic I will have just a handful of questions for you. First off you discussed Article 17 on the Law on Defence and the MUP. Would you agree with me that if Article 17 of the Law on Defence envisaged any change --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, my Witness Mladenovic did not mention Article 17 of the law. He spoke of other matters and this is being imputed to him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe he did discuss the MUP jurisdiction over the MUP -- resubordination of the MUP. If that's not Article 17 of the Law on Defence, then I don't know what is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's get your question which --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- This does not prevent you asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that if Article 17 of the Law on Defence envisaged any change in the regular course of affairs of the law relating to MUP personnel and jurisdiction over their discipline or prosecution for crimes once resubordinated to VJ commanders for combat, that there would have to be a legal act or article of the law explicitly changing the employment status of the MUP employee or jurisdiction over them. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, would you also agree with me that as far as you know, no such provision of the law exists at any level changing the jurisdiction over MUP employees in the event of resubordination to the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We did have this evidence yesterday quite clearly, without perhaps reference to Article 17, but the witness said clearly that there was no question of him having jurisdiction over the MUP at any stage and that that extended to disciplinary proceedings of all kinds I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I believe you also mentioned that citizens had the legal obligation to report any crime that they eye-witnessed. This may be obvious, but just to be clear, that obligation would continue to apply even when such a citizen were engaged or assigned to the VJ. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I never mentioned that citizens had any obligation to report. I think that yesterday I stated that they should report and anybody can file a criminal report or a criminal complaint, but I didn't speak of anybody's obligation to do so, I didn't yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that with respect to crimes for which punishment is envisioned as a prison sentence of five years or more there does exist an obligation for citizens to report such crimes if they witnessed them or are aware of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The duty of citizens to report crimes only exists in cases where either death penalty or 40 years' imprisonment is envisaged for such crimes. As for officials, authorised officials, then yes, they have the duty to report crimes of which they learned in the course of their official duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to authorised officials, am I correct that the precise details, the crime, identity, location, time, and other critical details need to be reported or recorded by such authorised officials even when such authorised officials are within the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they learn of such acts in the course of their duties. I can clarify, by your leave. If an authorised official wearing civilian clothes walks about and comes across a crime being committed of the gravity that I mentioned, then that person is not duty-bound to report it. However, if that person learns of such a crime in the course of their official duties, then yes, they do have the duty to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You'll see I'm waiting for the transcript to catch up with us, not questioning your answer. With respect to military police or security organs, in the course of undertaking their official duties, am I correct that they are authorised by the applicable criminal procedural law to detain and/or arrest persons undertaking such serious crimes, including MUP personnel?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military police, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, but rather the scope of their authority is actually regulated by the Law on Military Courts, but they were not authorised to arrest MUP members. In principle, yes, any citizen can arrest anyone else if they are caught committing a grave crime, but the military police did not have any jurisdiction over members of the MUP. They couldn't arrest them; they could only report them to the competent prosecutor, but not the military prosecutor. I don't know whether members of the military police came across such cases and whether they reported such crimes to the competent civilian prosecutor. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to cases where there is a reasonable suspicion to believe that some individual has participated or assisted in an attack on VJ personnel or property and when such persons are apprehended by VJ units, am I correct that the security organs of the VJ would be the appropriate and duly authorised organs to investigate and process the suspects further?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because this has to do with something that falls under their jurisdiction. They are authorised to uncover crimes and perpetrators who committed crimes against the Army of Yugoslavia. What you just described would constitute a crime against the Army of Yugoslavia, and in that case the military police has jurisdiction over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Mladenovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovic. I'll start --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- by asking you some questions about what Mr. Ivetic was just inquiring about. If I understood correctly, in 1998/1999 in Yugoslavia, Serbia, was there an obligation for any citizen who witnessed a crime for which either the death penalty or a 40-year sentence was applicable, was there a legal obligation for such a citizen to report a crime like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that a --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Only when it comes to the most serious crimes, it is only then that citizens, ordinary citizens, have a duty to report when they learn or eye-witness them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I want to clarify. What are these most serious crimes? Can you define them for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our criminal code from that period of time, those were crimes punishable by death penalty or a maximum prison sentence, which at that time was 20 years. The law stipulated that it pertained to crimes for which a death penalty could be pronounced. Only in those cases, when it came to those crimes, did the citizens have a duty to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1999 can you tell me what crimes those would be? Would that be certain kinds of murder? Would that include war crimes against civilians? Can you tell us which crimes those would be?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia, you have already mentioned the crime of qualified murder. One of the modes of a qualified murder is a murder of several persons. That is a qualified murder. A war crime against civilian population as a crime from the code as it existed at that time was not punishable by death penalty or the maximum prison sentence, which was 20 years at that time and 40 years nowadays. So according to our law it seems as though a war crime is a less serious crime than a murder of several persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a minimum number of persons required before the death penalty or the 20-year maximum would apply; and if so, what was that number?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least two persons. I'm referring to the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other kinds of murder to which the death penalty or the 20-year maximum applied in 1999, any other special kinds of circumstances? I don't know, a victim under the age of 15 or over the age of 70, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our law did not have such provisions at the time. However, when it comes to a qualified murder there are other modes as well, such as, for example, a murder committed out of hatred, vengeance, reckless vengeance and things like that, in a very brutal manner and so on. These are qualified murders from Article 47, paragraph 2 of the law at the time. The death penalty was envisaged at that time also for serious types of robbery, for example, armed robbery. If an armed robbery is carried out and somebody was killed with premeditation, then that was also a very serious crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Help me if you can. I heard from an earlier witness, we had some discussion about the death penalty. In 1999 my understanding was it was on the books, but as a practical matter it was or could not be applied. Is that right? Did that have something to do with whether it was the federal statute or the republic statute? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1999 the death penalty existed from a formal legal point of view. At the federal level the federal code envisaged it. Later on the federal law abolished it; however, the republican laws still had it. So for as long as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia existed - and you know that later on it was transformed into the Union of Serbia and Montenegro, that was in 1993 or 2003 - so the federal law did not envisage death penalty and this is where the problems arose. And to tell you the truth, I can't even remember when a death penalty was last carried out in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question. Even though it was on the books, as a practical matter was it ever actually sought or applied? And you tell me you can't remember the last time it happened.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't remember. As a substitute to death penalty, when in 2003 it was abolished by the federal criminal code, it was substituted by a 40-year prison sentence as a similar kind of punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, do you know when Yugoslavia joined the Council of Europe, of which it's now going -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an informed citizen, I might know it. I think it was in 2001. There was some kind of a suspension there. Our state's membership in international institutions was suspended for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Kamenova reminds me that, of course, as a member of the Council of Europe it would be impossible to carry out an execution, and Serbia did become a prominent member of the Council of Europe. I have one other question I would like to ask you. The murder of a soldier or the murder of a police officer, was either of these regarded as aggravated murders or were they simply regarded as murders of a citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Murders of a citizen. That's how it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, when you were explaining this obligation of a citizen to report a grave crime like the ones we've been talking about, I think you said either when they were an eye-witness or when they had learned of it. I take that to mean that they wouldn't necessarily have to be an eye-witness, but if they got information that would indicate to them that such a crime had taken place then they were obliged to report it under the law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult to speak of this, what you suggest, they learned about something going on and -- well, the question is what sort of information does one receive. If they eye-witness something, that's more likely to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me try a little hypothetical with you. I agree that it's probably a factual question that's going to be determined on an individual case-by-case basis, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if an individual discovered a mass grave with 20 bodies and the bodies showed signs of bullet wounds and someone told them he had killed those persons, that would probably be enough, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. There is a grave, so people are buried in the ground. How would it be possible to see bullet wounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in my hypothetical I'm assuming that the bodies were then unearthed and a physical examination was done to show those kind of bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand the specific question. Whose duty would it be to report something like that; is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, I would intervene to clarify this. If the bodies were not interred and there was no earth on the bodies and a few bodies were lying in a ditch in the shape of a grave and somebody sees it, I think what will happen, then he can see what's wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree under those circumstances you would probably have an obligation to report it, as it would appear to be a mass murder?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, it depends on all the circumstances, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. What you're putting to me now is a question of facts. So far all we've got to go on is a hypothesis, maybe someone killed those persons, but it's very difficult for me to address issues that are merely hypothetical or mere assumptions. If maybe you can name a specific incident or a specific case I could help you if it was something that I actually knew about because this is purely theatrical. I am here to give evidence about facts that are familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I think even though you and I probably went to different law schools we had the same professor who told us: Never say never and always say maybe, and that's the way good lawyers deal with matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that certainly rings a bell. Something might be the case but then not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. You mentioned that there's a possibility of a citizen's arrest regarding a grave crime. If I eye-witness, for example, a multiple murder, under the law, if I physically were capable of it, I can effect a citizen's arrest on the perpetrator of that crime? You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Otherwise your own life might be on the line; that's what the law says. Each citizen may arrest, and so on and so forth, and that's how it should be. There is the institute of extreme necessity or self-defence, of course. However, it is also a matter of one's physical capability because one must always make sure that one's own life is not in danger. So again ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. And a VJ soldier who saw a MUP member committing a multiple murder could effect a citizen's arrest legally, technically, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a soldier -- a soldier as a citizen you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In purely legal terms, yes. In purely physical terms, in realistic terms, if you like, well, that depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. This afternoon you said to Mr. Cepic regarding the statute of limitations on war crimes that -- I think your answer was that in principle or the principle is that that statute of limitations does not run. Is that set forth in a law or a decree somewhere in Serbia or the former Yugoslavia or is that just a matter of legal principle?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That is set forth in our laws, our criminal laws. I learned that when I was a student and I still remember that. I know the law says clearly that there is no statute of limitations on war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Does that then apply to any other types of crimes? Does that apply to qualified murder?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Qualified murder -- well, the statute of limitations applies to qualified murder, but it would take roughly twice as much time as the envisaged prison sentence, which at the time, let's say, was 20 years and then it was 40 later. For it to become some sort of rough equivalent to the death penalty, then it would have taken about 80 years. I'm talking about the absolute statute of limitations, because we distinguish in our country between the two different kinds of statutes, and I suppose it must be along the same lines in other systems as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned General Lazarevic started this requirement or procedure for investigative judges to attend at the sanitation of the terrain. When, approximately, did that start, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in early April 1999. There were orders by General Lazarevic at the time on sanitisation. There was an investigating judge who was dispatched, but as I said before I observed the fact that there was a great amount of risk involved, because three or four investigating judges face situations like that and I myself did once. So at one point I disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, if I may be of assistance here. Page 24, lines 24 and 25. The witness said that we in our country we differentiate between the absolute statute of limitations and the relative statute of limitations and he imagined it would be along the same lines in other jurisdictions. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes sense. Thanks for your help. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding the Mali Alas and the Slovinje cases, are you aware of whether or not either one of those cases had been re-opened and is being pursued by UNMIK?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that yesterday and we looked at that document showing that there was an investigation, local Serbs were being investigated about Slovinje and Mali Alas. I said today that the case file should be in the Council for War Crimes, which is attached to the Belgrade Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just before we break I'd like to show you one document, if I may, I've got a hard copy here in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or should we break now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. We've got another 15 minutes, Mr. Hannis. We started at 2.15 -- in fact, we were late in starting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Your Honour. I was thinking of another schedule. And, Your Honours, I have the English but I guess you don't. And I only have one copy at the moment. I don't know how you would like me to proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it worked fine with Mr. Cepic just reading what he needs to read to make it clear what's being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, this is what appears to be a judgement from the military court in Nis dated the 21st of November, 2003. If you want to look at the entire document and perhaps check the last page because it appears to have your name and signature as the presiding judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have a number for the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is P3083, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the hard copy of the document is there next to you, sir. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall this case? Are you familiar with this particular case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through a glass darkly, as they say. I've seen many cases. Perhaps we should look at the verdict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you want to go to page 2 of the English, there's a finding of guilty, I guess two individuals. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the first one is Vlatko Vukovic, retired colonel, and the charge against him was for inciting false injury in the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he was convicted for that, that very crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's all I wanted to do with you right now, is just confirm that this is an authentic document and an accurate reflection of the judgement you entered in that case on that date.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't me. It was the chamber of the military court and I happened to be its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the document record a sentence, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. In English we can -- it's page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, can you tell the Court what the sentence was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it on the next page, the suspended sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what sentence was imposed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have something called a suspended sentence. A prison sentence is pronounced, but then there is a probation period. If, for example, this person does not commit another crime within one year, the person never ends up going to prison and the sentence is never executed. So that is the gist of a suspended sentence, at least in your criminal code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's suspended for one year, is the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right below that I see that both the accused were obliged to pay a lump sum of 2.000 dinars. Is that a fine or is that court costs or what is that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the costs of the proceedings and this is not something that is imposed, but rather there is a lump sum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the person commits another offence within one year, how long does he spend in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the person commits this crime with intent, then this suspended sentence can be revoked and another sentence may be imposed for this new crime and then there can be another sentence for both crimes combined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand. Could you tell us again what the crime is in this instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Falsifying an official document. It is a crime that exists under the federal law, the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's rather different from the English we had already, falsifying an official document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the crime for which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Official, official, not private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I said in English; it must have been mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand reading the document, Your Honour, in English it appears the other accused Mr. Vukadinovic was found guilty of the crime of falsifying an official document under Article 184; and Mr. Vukovic or retired Colonel Vukovic was found guilty of incitement to falsify an official document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And what was the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was a suspended sentence of three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: It was a sentence for three months but it was suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what the document says, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know. But there is a sentence which is to be suspended, so that's why I wanted to inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's why I misunderstood. That's not the explanation that the witness has just given us. His explanation a moment ago was that if another crime is committed the whole thing is re-assessed and then a prison sentence is imposed. Now, that's different from imposing a sentence and suspending it for a year. So which is it, Mr. Mladenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is established that during the probation period the person commits another crime - and this must be established by a court ruling - then this three-month sentence is, so to speak, added to the sentence that the person will get for the other thing and then there is a combined prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I think I understand it, but it's different from the earlier English translation of the circumstances. And just to be clear about what this crime was again ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Falsifying official documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Incitement to falsify an official document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who actually perpetrated this crime was a sergeant and he falsified the document, but the colonel had incited him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the colonel that Mr. Hannis and I suspect we are interested in. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. One question about that. The document refers to Mr. Vukovic as a retired colonel, and this is a judgement in the military court. How does that work? He was in the army at the time the crime was committed, but it appears by the time the judgement is imposed he is now retired. So how is it that the army maintains jurisdiction over him? Is it because the indictment was filed before he left the army or how does that work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are crimes against officials committed by officers, for example. It doesn't matter if they will retire the next day. This is always under the jurisdiction of a military court. The Law on Military Courts states that in no uncertain terms. This is the exclusive jurisdiction of a military court. When an officer in the line of duty commits a crime violating his duty, falsifying official documents, accepting bribery, abuse of office, embezzlement or anything like that, this will always be something for a military court and that's why we tried this ex-military officer who was now retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That takes me to the next area I wanted to deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, Mr. Hannis. Does that mean that even if he had retired before the indictment was issued it would still have proceeded before the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, at page 103, line 7 of the transcript, you, in an answer, said: "The Pristina Corps command had jurisdiction over criminal matters when crimes were committed by military persons who were members of the corps and also in relation to some crimes committed by civilians against the army." Now, I have seen in a document from Colonel Delic about members of the 549th who were prosecuted --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, either my learned friend is receiving an erroneous interpretation of page 103 of yesterday's transcript or maybe there was a misinterpretation, because the Pristina Corps command can have no jurisdiction over -- that's what I see on page 31, lines 19 to 20. It can only be a military court; they cannot have jurisdiction over criminal matters. So the command is one thing and the military court is another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it's the very first words of the quotation: "The Pristina Corps command had jurisdiction ..." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is what it says, Your Honour, but I think I picked up in the middle of the sentence. He said: "The courts that were set up and attached to certain commands - in this specific case the Pristina Corps command had jurisdiction over criminal matters where crimes were committed by military persons." And perhaps there should be another dash after that "command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: What about members of other corps or armies temporarily attached or resubordinated to the Pristina Corps? Did your court, your military court in the Pristina Corps command, have jurisdiction over those individuals even though they may have been members of a different corps or even a different army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military court that was attached to the Pristina Corps command had jurisdiction over units from other corps as well in as far as they were resubordinated to the Pristina Corps command because all these are military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So is it correct, then, that in Kosovo during the war in 1999 your court -- for any crimes committed by VJ personnel in Kosovo during that time-period, your court had jurisdiction over them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if they were actually part of the Pristina Corps. As I said yesterday, members of the air force were no longer under our jurisdiction but delegation was possible. And I think I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess what I'm not clear on is the situation regarding certain units from outside Kosovo. We have evidence about the 37th Brigade, the 252nd, the 72nd Special Brigade from Belgrade, the 63rd Parachute Brigade. Is it a matter of whether or not they were officially resubordinated to the Pristina Corps that causes jurisdiction to arise for you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talk about jurisdiction it is more a question of personal territorial jurisdiction. If there were any such units in Kosovo and Metohija, jurisdiction over persons or total jurisdiction, and these units were never resubordinated to the corps command. I don't know where the military courts would be that would be responsible for those members. But if a crime like that is committed then there can be delegation of criminal proceedings. You mentioned the 37th. Well, I think we actually prosecuted a great number of their members, and this is a unit that was at one point resubordinated. The 37th Brigade of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the members of military territorial detachments or units, were they under the jurisdiction of the ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not under the jurisdiction of the court over which I presided but rather of the other one that was attached to the military district command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And reservist, army reservist, who would they fall under? I guess that depends on what unit they actually joined and participated with, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they weren't independent; they were part of some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us, and I've seen in some of the documents that under certain circumstances the military court had jurisdiction over civilians for certain kinds of crimes if it were a crime against the army or against army personnel, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I take it that would apply equally to a MUP member who committed a crime against either the army or army personnel, if a MUP soldier shot or assaulted a VJ member?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday, didn't I? In a given situation a MUP member is exactly the same as any other civilian. If he commits a crime against the army, he will be tried by a military court; if he kills a member of the army who is acting in an official capacity, he will be tried in a military court. But, for example, if he kills him in a pub, then he won't be tried by a military court but rather by a civilian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is this the appropriate time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Mladenovic, we have to break at this stage for 20 minutes. Could you meanwhile leave the courtroom, please, with the usher. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, before I continue on, I wanted to go back to one thing we were discussing earlier, that obligation to report certain grave crimes. You told us that was a legal obligation. Was there a penalty in the law for failing to report under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Is it on now? It is. In the criminal code there is a crime of failure to report a crime and its perpetrator. When it was stated in the code that the most serious crimes have to be reported, then the code also prescribed what constituted a crime of failure to report, and there are these types of crimes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know off the top of your head what article that is in the criminal code?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never came across such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Between your military court and the Pristina Corps command and the military court for the Pristina Military District, it seems that in 1999 there could have been some overlap of jurisdictions between those two courts regarding, for example, crimes committed by civilians against the army. Is that right? It seems that some of those could have been tried in either one of those two courts.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle and also when it comes to the jurisdiction, the military court with the military district command had jurisdiction over civilians who committed crimes against members of the military. However, there were also rules of the procedure that were applied during the times of war, and one of the provisions envisaged that another court could prosecute for these crimes and have jurisdiction in cases where those crimes committed by civilians were aimed at members of the units where such a court was established. So there was no overlap there. There was a provision authorising such a court, in this particular case it was the court of the Pristina Corps, to prosecute civilians if they committed crimes against members of that corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- ask a question for clarification. It's not quite clear to me from the answer given whether or not there is a penalty for failure to report a crime. Unfortunately, the way the answer was given, it's not quite clear. Could it be clarified for me, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is no crime for which punishment is not envisaged. There was a punishment envisaged for the failure to report a crime, but I couldn't tell you exactly what sentence it was. We could look at the law itself and see there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, I understand the VJ had some civilian employees, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were civilians employed in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were they subject to jurisdiction of the military courts as on an equal basis with VJ members?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They were civilians, civilian persons, as the name indicates, and the military court had jurisdiction over them just like in cases of other civilians if they committed crimes against members of the army or in the course of their duties, official duties. If a civilian employed in the army inflicted grave injury on someone, then that person would not be tried by a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday at page 104, line -- beginning at line 10 you mentioned that the military courts have jurisdiction over military personnel, enumerating them by category, and you said policemen aren't listed there. What about civil defence and civil protection personnel, are they considered non-military for purposes of your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in some certain combat orders, documents, we've seen referenced to a group called the armed non-Siptar population. I take that in your view that's not something that would be considered personnel under the VJ military courts' jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you. Do you mean armed or non-armed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I mean armed, and it's the term used in these documents is armed non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they were considered civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked a question, I think, from one of the Judges about the situation where you might have a military person on duty committing a crime along with a civilian, the two of them committing a crime against another civilian. And you told us -- you explained that if they are accomplices then the military court has some jurisdiction; if they are co-perpetrators, the military court remains in charge always in such cases. Is there -- maybe it's a translation issue. There any difference for you between the term "co-perpetrator" and "accomplice" in that context?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see now that in my evidence yesterday I had a slip of the tongue. If a civilian and a military person commit a crime together and this crime is not the one over which only a military court has jurisdiction, then both the civilian and the military person will be tried by civilian court. Specifically speaking, if an officer and a civilian inflict a grave bodily injury on someone, then both the officer and the civilian person will be tried before a civilian court that would try the civilian. And I apologise for my slip yesterday. However, if an officer commits a crime in the line of duty violating his official duty and a civilian was an accomplice who either instigated or was an accessory, then the military court would try both the officer and the civilian because that particular crime falls under exclusive jurisdiction of the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there certain kind of conduct by, for example, that military officer that would convert or take him outside the line of duty? For example, I mean his duty may be to search in a certain area for terrorists, but if in the course of doing that he rounds up civilians and shoot some or orders subordinates to shoot some, is he still acting within the line of duty or does that mere act take him outside the line of duty. Do you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With -- despite all the intellectual effort I put into this, I fail to understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That may be a particular problem of mine because of the jurisdiction I come from and certain civil law issues. I'll pass on that and move on to something else. In one of your answers yesterday, you were talking about the possibility if resubordination of the MUP had taken place and what disciplinary liability might attach. I wasn't clear from your answer then, do you draw a distinction between discipline and more serious violations or crimes or are you referring to the whole range of misconduct from a breach of the Rules of Service to a war crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was clear. There is a difference between disciplinary and some other kind of responsibilities such as criminal responsibility. A disciplinary responsibility is a lighter or more serious violation of military discipline, and we all know what criminal responsibility entails. Yesterday I did not address whether there were any resubordination or in cases of resubordination of members of the MUP to a military unit or a corps. All I said was the system of disciplinary responsibility was not identical, that there were differences, that different regulations regulated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understood that answer yesterday to mean that if there had been resubordination because of those differences between the army and the MUP systems of discipline, you didn't think as a practical matter even if they had been resubordinated that the VJ could have disciplined MUP members who were acting with the army under that resubordination order. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a complex question. It depends on the mode of resubordination, if there was resubordination. And the person issuing an order to resubordinate needs to regulate these issues in that order. To resubordinate MUP units to a military unit, it is not sufficient for the Supreme Defence Council as a collective supreme commander to make such a decision because there is another side to this with split competences. There are republican institutions and federal institutions involved, and if they fail to agree among themselves then there can be no discussion of any resubordination there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You were asked about who had the authority to file criminal reports. You told us in principle anybody could. In real life who usually filed criminal reports? Was it usually designated officials?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the criminal reports in the cases that we have discussed here were filed by members of the military police and members of the security organs from the corps. What I know is that every brigade in the territory of Kosovo had a military police unit. I think that they were at least the size of a company, and they also had security organs within their units. Naturally, security organs cannot be aware of every single incident. When we discuss criminal reports, when we say "criminal reports," then we are referring to the final act of submitting a report to the military prosecutor. And the person who did file this criminal report with the military prosecutor probably learned about the incident from a member of the unit or perhaps from some soldiers who were out there in the field. I'm just supposing this. I can't claim this with certainty, because in the document I can only see the signature of the person filing the report. Now, as to how that person learned about the pertinent information that is contained in the criminal report, I suppose that that person learned it through the skills applied in his job, the job that he was tasked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In principle, though, a civilian could initiate a complaint, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't have any personal knowledge of that ever having happened in 1999, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, that's a factual issue, and I do have such information. I personally as a president of the court was approached by a citizen in Nis, an Albanian, who reported to me that his vehicle had been stolen. I think that that person was an employee of the municipal court in Pristina. I remember that well. I remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the only one, though, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was reported to me as the president of the court. I don't know how many such reports reached prosecutors. He reported this to me. I sent it to the prosecutor, and the case was prosecuted in term -- meaning that the perpetrator was identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mladenovic, you told us yesterday that if an officer of the army reports a crime, then his obligation ceases once he reported it, he doesn't have any further obligation; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing prescribed by regulations, no, no further duty. As for other obligations not prescribed by law, I don't think we need to discuss that. It -- he wasn't able to. In accordance with our existing provisions, he could not follow up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What form did that report have to take? Was it merely enough to orally advise a military policeman or was it required to fill out some kind of written form or were there any rules about how that report was to be made by the military officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely to make it easier to identify perpetrators and to prosecute them. A criminal report or a criminal complaint does not have a specified form, prescribed form. It is sufficient to report something verbally, whatever one learns can be reported verbally. The military police people did have some forms, but it's not enough for there to be just a verbal account for the prosecutor to take additional steps. There has to be some reasonable suspicion -- doubt that something had happened, that there's a certain degree of veracity in order for this to be taken further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You described for us yesterday a little bit about how the process worked of the initial receiving of a criminal report. At page 109 beginning at line 9 you talked about the stages. You mentioned the pre-criminal case where the investigative judge and the military police investigate, and then you mention a separate proceeding or stage called preliminary proceedings. What are those? Is that something that takes place before an indictment is filed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what's the relevance of this detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that we've had it before and I'm just trying to get the process clear for purposes of dealing with the cases that we do have; and we'll talk about later on. I know I'm nearing the end of my time, and I can move on to something more of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm just trying to see why the detail of the procedure matters to the issues that we're considering. If you can tell me, then obviously that would be justification for this; but if it's just for the sake of completeness, it isn't necessarily a good reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is our position that there were certain things that did not get processed the way that we believed they should have based on the information they had, and understanding the process will help us identify how and where the failure may have taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try and speed it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you recall my question about the criminal proceedings. What are those that take place before an indictment is filed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand your question, but I have a correction to make. An investigative judge in the pre-criminal proceedings does not appear except when an on-site investigation is conducted before any pre-criminal proceedings begin, otherwise he has no obligation to appear only the military police and the prosecutor do. The purpose of this pre-criminal proceedings is to find valid information that would enable the prosecutor to ask the court to start the proceedings, and this is something that we call investigation or investigative proceedings. And it is only then that an investigative judge comes on the scene. And once he establishes that matters have been clarified enough, the file is sent to the prosecutor, who then decides whether to issue an indictment or drop charges. This is briefly what these proceedings are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it necessary to have an order from an investigative judge to carry out an exhumation or could that be done by the military police or the military prosecutor without involving an investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only an investigative judge is authorised to order exhumation and post mortem of a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, Your Honour, there was a portion of the transcript that you requested further clarification of the translation and I think that was at page 109, lines 23 or 24, there was a reference to a wink and a nod. I don't know if you got a clarification of that. I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These clarifications don't come for weeks now and after the event, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless you specifically ask for it immediately, and we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, yesterday you indicated that during your 11 years as a military court judge no one attempted or had any influence on your work, and then you had -- an answer was translated as: "It was more likely to have a wink-and-a-nod kind of suggestion to help one accused over another." Is that what you said; and if so, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a case of a singularly bad interpretation. There was no wink and a nod. I mentioned nothing of the sort. I said verbatim that none of the people from the military establishment ever tried to influence me as a judge.
