It was more of a case where on a friendly basis - and by this I'm referring to the fact that we judges do not exist in a vacuum, we are not anti-social people, we socialise, we see other people, we are entitled to that just like any other citizen - so in these social contacts occasionally one of those friends would inquire, show interest, in a case or in a person, and that cannot be qualified as attempt to influence or any influence. I don't know whether any of my colleagues, judges, or prosecutors could say that they were never asked by, say, a neighbour about the fate of a particular case or something of the sort. That's what I wanted to say yesterday, and I just repeated it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you didn't view those friendly inquiries as any attempt to influence you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I would like to ask one or two questions. Judge, I just wanted to know, your routine meetings with the corps commander, how frequent were these meetings and were you following a routine? Did you go to him or he came to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very beginning of the war, perhaps I would go once or twice a week to these meetings with the commander, and then the commander said that there was no need for me to come to these meetings where issues were discussed that I knew nothing about. I am not a strategist and that it was sufficient for us to speak occasionally on the phone, and should there be a problem in the functioning of the court that I should warn him directly and immediately. And what we saw here, the regular reporting in writing was done on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Why would you go to those meetings when you did go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to inform those who were present about the crime rate and the situation with the crimes and the court, to inform them about the activities of the court. And as I have said, I only came once or twice a week in the beginning of the war, I attended those meetings on that basis; and then after that -- actually, it was no duty of mine, nobody tasked me with this, it's just that I thought personally that it was my duty to come to those meetings once I learned that there would be a meeting. Nobody ordered me or instructed me to come to these meetings. Once the commander saw me present there, he said to me there was no need for me to be there; and that if there was a need, it was sufficient for me to inform him on the phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, an independent judge will not pursue like this and go to meetings when he's not even wanted. Why did you do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an independent judge, but at the same time I'm the president of the court, and I'm responsible for ensuring that the court functions properly. Where would I go for assistance if not to a meeting of the corps command? I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You didn't have ministerial staff like a registrar or somebody to work on that side for arranging logistics for requesting for help instead of the judge going himself and sitting beside all these people who were a party before him in the course of adjudication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know on what basis you believe them to be party to proceedings. They could potentially be so because the court has competencies over them as well, but there never was a case where I went to see a party to the proceedings. As for a registrar of the court or somebody of that nature, I have to remind you that this was wartime, and there are no provisions ensuring that the court would have a registrar in charge of logistics. I think that I have told you that the court established at the corps command did not have its funds, just as today the courts today in Serbia do not have their budget that would enable them to buy all the material and supplies they need for your work. No, the funds existed at the level of the corps only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, you mentioned yesterday that during the war - this is at page 111, line 19 - you conducted investigations of about -- the first answer was translated as 8.000, later corrected to 1.000 persons. Over 900 of those were eventually indicted. Is that correct, you had over 90 per cent indictment rate on cases investigated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is true that there were 1.000 requests to conduct an investigation. I didn't say that the court managed to conduct all of those investigations, and there were indictments, both indictments and motions to indict, because not in all cases is an indictment issued. So there were indictments against 900 people; however, we have to bear in mind that in cases where a crime was punishable with a sentence of ten years, the prosecutor could issue an indictment without previously conducting an investigation. This is why this figure seems quite substantial, but there were also cases where indictment was issued without a prior investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that answer mean that 900 indictments were issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 900 indictments or motions to indict; yes against 900 persons. I'm not saying there were 900 indictments; it's just that against 900 persons indictments were issued for both courts, not just the court over which I presided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not clear either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the difference between an indictment and a motion to indict?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understand why this is difficult for you to understand when it comes to this. A motion to indict is a document, a procedural document by a competent prosecutor who is authorised to issue it without conducting an investigation previously to that, and that can be only done in cases of minor crimes punishable by up to three years in peace and by up to ten [as interpreted] years in war in cases where the prosecutor has sufficient foundation to indict. So out of these 1.000 investigations conducted in both courts, not all of them were finalised and indictments issued in those cases; rather, this number of indictments includes those that were issued without a prior investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do those motions to indict done without prior investigation have to be reviewed and approved by a judge before the case continues or does it go directly to a trial without anything further?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to motions to indict, in wartime they could be issued for crimes punishable with up to five years of imprisonment, and in those cases, one could proceed immediately with the trial. As for indictments themselves there were preliminary motions that could be raised in relation to those indictments; and if there were such preliminary motions, then they were reviewed by three professional judges. If there were no preliminary motions, then they proceeded to trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, we're getting very complicated now. A moment ago you were recorded in English as saying that in wartime the motion to indict procedure could apply where up to ten years in prison was the penalty. You've now said it was up to five years' imprisonment according to this transcript. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we need to correct, not in the case of a motion to indict, but an indictment -- so if it's up to ten years, then they needed an indictment but without an investigation. And when it comes to motions to indict, then it's with -- for crimes punishable up to five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is now incomprehensible to me, Mr. Hannis, I'm afraid. In page 49, line 6 -- just a second - the answer is: "A motion to indict is a procedural document by a prosecutor who's authorised to issue it without conducting an investigation and that can only be in the case of minor crimes punishable by up to three years in peace and up to ten years in war in cases where the prosecutor has sufficient foundation to indict." Now, did you mean to say five years there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five years, in wartime, five years; and in peacetime up to three years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Out of the thousand investigations which were conducted, how many of these led to an indictment? Now, we understand they're not the motion-to-indict types of cases, but how many of them resulted in an indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how many because not all of them were finalised in wartime. I said that they were pending, they were in progress during wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what the percentage of indictment was after the war was concluded, I don't have such information. Out of those 900, some of them were as a result of an investigation that had been conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many of the 900 were the result of an investigation conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could give you only an approximate answer because I did not prepare myself for this, but there were certain cases; but I couldn't tell you exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us yesterday at page 112, line 10, that about 230 of these 900 constitute violations of the international laws of war, and then you were asked what kinds of crimes predominantly. And you said: "Various forms of murder, robbery, theft, aggravated theft, vehicles being seized, sex-related offence ..." Are all those crimes crimes that are considered violations of international laws of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, they could be subsumed under that heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, my learned friend probably misquoted. It's not violations of international laws of war, but humanitarian law because that was what we said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the transcript was corrected. I'm reading from page 112, line 6, in Mr. Cepic's question: "Mr. Mladenovic, if you were dealing with crimes that potentially constituted violations of the international laws of war, how many indictments like that did you have? I know you can't be all that specific." And the answer was: "About 230 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, could we please check the tape to be sure what was said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I have the answer from the witness that in his opinion those could be subsumed under that heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- let's be clear. What's the difference between the two, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, what's the difference between the international laws of war and the international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this feels sort of like an exam at the law faculty. We're talking about the violation of convention and crimes against the civilian population when we refer to violations of the humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you should explore this to the extent necessary to clarify the point. I don't think going back over yesterday's transcript will necessarily help. We are now alerted to a problem, apparently, and you can resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, in what circumstances would you consider the crime of theft or vehicle theft to be a violation of either international law of war or international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could be taken to be that. It's a crime against property owned by citizens in the area we are discussing, and it could have a certain degree that this was about a violation of humanitarian law, theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what makes it different? Is it because the property's taken by a soldier from a civilian during a time of war? Is that how you would distinguish from just a plain, ordinary theft prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you speak English, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't. I studied Russian in both elementary and secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you understand? You seem to answer pretty quickly sometimes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned some specific cases yesterday that you were familiar with, one of them regarded Major Petrovic and two other soldiers who were charged with murder. Did you deal with that case personally?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war a request because made to launch an investigation of Major Petrovic and two other soldiers about that crime in a qualified form. I was the president of the courts, and I received information from a military police officer that someone had tampered with the bodies of the persons who had been killed. I issued an order for this to be looked into, and then we knew with a greater degree of certainty that this had been done by Major Petrovic. It was later, when I was already a military court judge in Nis, that I handled that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And there's a case involving Major Mancic. Do you have personal involvement in that case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before moving to that. Mr. Mladenovic, Petrovic was sentenced to nine years -- nine years? Sorry, what is it you said he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An investigation was carried out that he was the instigator behind these two soldiers killing a married couple, so this was aggravated murder. That's what the investigation was about. It wasn't until later that he was actually accused of a war crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've asked you that because the English translation was that someone had tampered with the bodies, so -- and I guessed it had been done by Petrovic, but that clearly isn't the basis for the conviction. You've clarified it. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there something else you wanted to say about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This tampering with the bodies or moving the bodies gave us a greater degree of certainty in terms of Major Petrovic being the one who had ordered for those persons to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. With regard to Major Mancic, were you personally involved in his case: It involved charges of war crimes against civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A conviction was reached before the military court, and they were sentenced to many years in prison. These are two officers and two soldiers, and the supreme military court that existed at the time imposed this sentence and increased the sentence. When the military courts were abolished, the Supreme Court of Serbia quashed this conviction and took the whole thing back to square one. Now I am the president of a chamber that is supposed to re-try these two officers and two soldiers for a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that's a case that's actively pending before you now?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we say a pending case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then maybe I shouldn't discuss details of it with you, but I do have a question. I understand at the time he was a major, I understand now that he's a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think my learned friend Mr. Hannis himself previously expressed reservations about this, questions about cases that are afoot or trials that are afoot, especially if the witness here happens to be the president of that chamber. I think this might constitute a serious interference with the principle of independence of the judiciary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why did you ask him about it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only asked him about the existence of that case and whether it was an ongoing case, that was the extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Mancic. More precisely my question -- why? Because there were war crimes that were discovered after the end of the war. Major Mancic was not on the list of war crimes that we have here in our case file in P955, the analysis that was drawn up by General Vojovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what's your response to the objection that you shouldn't be looking at any of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think my question asking about what his rank is really doesn't have any bearing on the facts of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, then it's irrelevant to us then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think I may have an argument to make about the fact that this man has been investigated, indicted, and charged with war crimes and he gets promoted by the army during the interim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would your argument be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my argument would be in jurisdictions I'm familiar with a policeman or an official who is charged with a crime typically gets suspended until those matters are resolved, and normally they're not getting promoted, not for a crime of this level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but just because it happens in jurisdictions you're familiar with, what then is the -- what's the point you would make? I mean, your jurisdiction might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My jurisdiction might be wrong, Your Honour, but I think there's other evidence that we've heard and in the documents that we've seen that how professional officers are treated when they're charged with crimes and sentenced with a crime, it's different than what happens with a conscript or a regular soldier or a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, it might be a good idea to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Mladenovic, until we resolve the issue between counsel. What do you mean it might be a good idea. You're now withdrawing your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is about the question and if the argument is that the army promoted someone who was indicted of war crimes, my question would be: Let us clarify when this crime was uncovered and when it was prosecuted. Maybe that doesn't affect independence of the court. We don't interfere with the trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection's withdrawn. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, do you what rank Mr. Mancic currently holds?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mancic, as far as I know, was thrown out of the army. He's no longer a professional soldier. The rank at the time was lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when he was promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I can answer your question. If during the war he was a major and then under the law he needed perhaps another five or six months in order to be promoted to lieutenant-colonel, there would have been no impediment for a regular procedure to have taken effect and for him to be promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel, since the crime that he is being charged with was not uncovered until much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when the crime against him was uncovered and when a charge was first brought?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in the habit of commenting until I have inspected a case file. As for individual cases, well, to be quite frank, I don't really try to memorise them. I always inspect a case file before I go into a courtroom. Therefore, I don't really know when the indictment was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would an entry number give you any information about when a case was filed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at a document, this is Exhibit P962, which I believe came from Colonel Delic. He's listed as the person responsible for the accuracy of this list of filed criminal reports against perpetrators in the 549th Motorised Brigade between May 1998 and July 1999; it's entry number 103, and it lists Mancic as a major and the entry number is 2696/00. Does that mean it was filed sometime in 2000?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it would mean, but only in relation to that particular register. I'm not sure if you have the court register or is this something that was kept by this unit commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I believe this is something only prepared and delivered by Colonel Delic. All right. Thank you. We'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, do we have a date when he was promoted as a colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have that information. I don't know if the witness knew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know that his professional service with the army was terminated, but I don't know of anything else. He was thrown out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You said he was promoted before the case was uncovered and how do you -- on what basis are you suggesting this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you -- you said you didn't know when he became a lieutenant-colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, no, he explained that the case had not been uncovered yet, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. President, may I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that he was promoted, he probably was, but what I'm saying is this: If he was a major back in 1999 needing another six months, for example, to make it to the rank of lieutenant-colonel, well he could as well have been promoted because we didn't know about the charges at the time, about the proceedings, about what we know now. I never said I knew when he was promoted. I don't know. I'm not in charge of human resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we must be nearing the end surely?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to specific cases, the report we have from the Nis prosecutor's office regarding -- it's Exhibit P954, Your Honours, and it's a 20 August 2001 report to the supreme military court in Belgrade. It includes a list of cases regarding unknown perpetrators, where there were multiple murders. One of the cases refers to approximately 95 bodies found in Orahovac. Are you familiar with that case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what the status of that investigation is now?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I do. I think this is more a question for the prosecutor. This is not an investigation. You only have an investigation when a perpetrator is known. These are investigative steps that are being taken in order to find out who the perpetrator is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And not included on this list is a matter involving over 100 bodies that were found near Izbica. You're familiar with that case, are you not, or that investigation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the bodies were found there. I believe that there is an observation in the document that you have about the stage these proceedings had reached by the time the report was drawn up. While I was with the military court I was involved with my assistants in drafting that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, Mr. Hannis, before you take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There was a matter which you had said that you would leave at page 39, lines 2 to 9, which the witness had said challenged all his intellectual effort. And you gave up. I wonder if you could revisit that question because I am interested to know the answer to that question myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll certainly try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would present the question to the witness in a form that he can readily comprehend you, seeing as he said he had a disability in fully understanding the nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, when we were talking about this before I was giving you a hypothetical situation where a military officer might engage in criminal activity while he's on duty and in uniform, for example, lining up civilians and shooting them during the course of assisting the MUP in an anti-terrorist operation. Does the fact that he's now committed a criminal act remove him from the jurisdiction of the military court because the military says, You're not acting like a soldier anymore so you're going to be tried in the civilian courts, or do you retain jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please, that at least is clear. If the hypothesis is correct, he's an officer of the VJ who does this, there are civilians, and he shoots them obviously a military court will have jurisdiction over something like this. He's an officer of the army, that's the first thing; and the second thing is he committed this crime. If indeed such a thing had happened, this would have been under the jurisdiction of a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if I answered your question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think that answers what I was interested in knowing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Cepic, is there re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, it's me again. Mr. Ivetic asked you about Article 17 of the Law on Defence, about resubordination. He put something to you in that question which I wasn't entirely clear about, therefore I will seek your clarification. Let's assume that there is resubordination of MUP members to the VJ. Can police officers become soldiers in that case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a case of real resubordination but resubordination in the proper sense of the word, for example, you have MUP bodies that become part of the corps, for example. By the same token the police officers would no longer be soldiers, but the Law on Military Courts at the time extended this particular jurisdiction and the military court would have been responsible for trying a person who was performing a military duty. So since they were resubordinated or if they were resubordinated, then of course they were part of a VJ unit, and thereby will be performing certain military duties. In that sense the Law on Military Courts stipulates that a military court can, indeed, try such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, during the war did you at any time receive any information indicating that a MUP unit had been resubordinated to the army, thereby extending your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P3083, it's an OTP exhibit. This is the sentence in the case of Colonel Vlatko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We heard about the punishment that pronounced. For a punishment like that, how long after can this be struck from the record? How long after is it expunged?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a probation period, normally a year, and then what it takes is another year after that, totalling two years after a conviction takes effect. There is a two-year period, provided of course the person does not commit another crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. And what does one do in that case with a sentence like this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other state bodies can deem this person to have no criminal record in the sense of being previously sentenced. But if this person is being tried by a court, this will not take effect; he will be considered as having been sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find that very confusing, Mr. Cepic. I don't know what any of that means. What -- the word that's been used in English is "expunged," how long after is it expunged. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Actually, in English the means is deleting from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean if you commit a crime like this --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- two years later you don't have any criminal record at all? Is that the position? Just a second. Is that the position, Mr. Mladenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If you commit a crime like this, but if a sanction is imposed on me in terms of a suspended sentence, then a two-year period is there, and during this two-year period this sanction is stricken from a criminal file or the criminal records kept by the appropriate bodies. And the person is viewed as not having been sentenced, at least in proving this before a state body. For example, if this person is looking for a job, then he can show that he has no criminal record. But if another crime is committed and then a new trial begins, this person can be considered to have been sentenced. But for other purposes, the person will be considered as not having been sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if three years after this sentence -- this suspended sentence he commits another crime that's identical, can the court take account of the fact that he previously was convicted and got a suspended sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this was the -- I got it now. A court will consider that person to have a prior conviction, but in any other state organ, any other state organ will not consider this person to have a previous conviction. However, any court will consider this person to have a previous conviction, and he will be considered as a repeat offender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This crime in this particular case, in B/C/S I think on page 49 or perhaps penultimate page, page 99, let me ask you this: What was the gravity of the crime for which Vukovic was convicted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR MLADENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This crime is punishable with a prison sentence from three months to five years. This is considered a lighter crime or a less serious crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If we have the page number 1 and page number 2 of this document, please, in B/C/S. Meanwhile --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we need to explore this any further with the witness, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, just one question with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This punishment, this sentence that Vukovic received, how grave is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it speaks for itself, Mr. Cepic. It's not appropriate for a court like us to explore the details of a sentence in another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I haven't got any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, by your leave, just two sentences, please, before I leave, if I may, may I, before I leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It depends what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank you for enabling me to come here and take part in these proceedings, to get to know the Tribunal, which will be of great importance for me in my future work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you asked us to consider granting audience to Mr. Petrovic for the examination of the Witness Petkovic on your list, in view of the pressure on you as you draw the Defence case for Mr. Lazarevic to an end. We've considered that application, we note the various undertakings given, and we will grant your application in the exceptional circumstances that exist at this time. You have indicated that the list of witnesses for this week was not, in fact, a final list and you have in mind to add another witness. You tell us that the time estimated to take the evidence of that witness is four hours. Now, you already are in a position where you don't have four hours and you have a number of witnesses before this one. So what we invite you to do is give consideration to the question how you are going to better manage the conclusion of the presentation of your case. We're not minded to tell you you can't have a particular witness if he was on your list, but you have to find a means within reason of leading the remaining evidence that you say you require. Now, it's obvious to us - I hope I'm not speaking out of turn - but it will be obvious to everybody in this courtroom that Vukovic will be subject to longer cross-examination than any other of the witnesses that remain for reasons which are based on the extent to which he's been mentioned already in the case and his involvement and also bearing in mind the length of his statement. So your view, which I understand you hold, that even allowing for Mr. Stefanovic you can probably finish your case this week is, I think, is ill-founded unless you re-arrange the timing certainly of his evidence and do what you can to confine the live evidence of other witnesses who are being presented along with 92 ter statements. So please give that some thought as you draw near the end. Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Lukic is not there, is he? No. The -- it follows that your case will certainly begin early next week at the latest. I doubt if it's going to begin this week, but if it does emerge that you are on at the end of this week, if there is an opening, then it can take place then. I don't know if that is your intention or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A problem with that would be, Your Honour, that we've had to fight with VWS to get witnesses to come here Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not suggesting -- well, I didn't know that you'd arranged that because you gave us no indication that there would be witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not this week, but the witnesses are arriving on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. All I'm saying to you is that if any part of your case has to be presented this week, then it would be your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we choose to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you have to have in mind that next week you will undoubtedly be leading evidence. I can't at this stage obviously say when, but from possibly Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's been our anticipation for some time and we will be ready to proceed next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Tuesday it would be -- whenever the court and other Defence case concludes and whenever the Court asks us to proceed, we will be ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next witness, Mr. Cepic, will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The next witness is already mentioned, Colonel Vlatko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that, in fact, the order -- the last line-up you gave us?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was notified of early Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That they were moving Gergar back and Vukovic up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what I suggest is that we break now and come back at 6.00 with Mr. Vukovic already in place so that we can have as much time as possible with him this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I've been waiting for you, good evening.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I've been waiting for you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did give a statement to the Defence team of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance, please, to pass this statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to put the same questions to you, or rather, to put the questions that were put to you when you gave your statement, would you provide identical answers?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly would provide identical answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender into evidence 5D1401, which is the statement of Witness Vlatko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you -- oh, sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we request that remain under seal for now until we can redact references to two protected witnesses that may reveal their identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you will deal with that in conjunction with Mr. Cepic, will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I can indicate for now the paragraphs that pertain if that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you should liaise with him and try to have a redacted version produced for tomorrow if that can be done, if it's simple as deleting certain paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that reminds me that we didn't deal with the situation affecting the Witness Gavrilovic, some of whose evidence was taken in private session. And Mr. Stamp dealt with that, I think; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that might have been Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it was Ms. Carter. Well, she should do exactly as Mr. Stamp is required to do in the case of Antic and provide a redacted version -- sorry -- yes, should consider the transcript and make a filing indicating the extent to which the transcript requires to remain confidential, under seal, and if she hasn't any court commitment for the remainder of this cross-examination -- the cross-examination of Lazarevic witnesses, then she could perhaps do that by Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll remind her. She is scheduled for the Witness Petkovic, but I don't think that's a very long proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So this statement will remain for the moment under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, do you have any convictions, criminal convictions?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for interpretation. Yes, I have been convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We speak the same language, so make sure you observe the pauses between question and answer. What were you convicted for?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand the crime, it was instigation in falsifying or forging an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you please give us the facts. What happened and what led to that, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to put it briefly because the judgement is quite long, but to put it briefly I ordered my subordinate to issue a receipt for fuel that we used for civilian buses which transported the army personnel on their tasks as a fuel for military vehicles. Naturally, my brigade commander was informed of all of this. Now, as to how a criminal complaint came to be written, I don't know. I have no information concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The fuel that was used, how much fuel was used as compared to what your unit daily used?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was negligible. Depending on any given day and the tasks of my unit, sometimes on a daily basis we used over 2.000 litres of fuel; and as far as I can remember in this particular case it involved 80 to 100 litres of fuel. I can't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We don't want to put the judgement on the screen, but it was stated that court costs in this particular case amounted to 2.000 dinars. How much was it in euros at the time and currently?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 2.000 dinars is approximately 25 euros, perhaps less than 25 euros.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, we heard here in the courtroom that in the morning on the 25th of March, 1999, as you were setting out to carry out an assignment in the broader area of Orahovac, you addressed your soldiers with the following words: Not a single Albanian ear should remain. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not true, and I never issued tasks to soldiers, but rather to those who were directly subordinated to me. I especially didn't issue any tasks on the 25th because as far as I can remember we set out at around 1.30 to carry out our assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said 1.30, do you mean a.m. or p.m.? We need it for the record.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: 1.30 in the military jargon means always a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your military log-book marked as P2010 in this case, or rather, 21 -- 2019, on the date of 25th of March, 1999, there is an entry saying that you cleansed the following villages: Bela Crkva, Celina, and others. I'd like to know the following: Did the units under your command carry out this task in the village of Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Combat Group 2, which was under my command at the time, on the 25th of March, 1999, had no combat engagements in the village of Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, be cautious in your use of this document because it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'm interested in this counter-terrorist action aimed at destroying Siptar terrorist forces starting on the 25th and onwards, I'm referring to the month of March. During that action did you have any contacts with civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contacts with civilians on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do in those situations?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In those situations I always sent civilians, or rather, pulled them out of the area where combat activities were carried out. I can elaborate on this if we have sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have very limited time. I'd simply like to know whether you talked to civilians in addition to these activities that you stated. Did you talk to any of them personally?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to them personally, to civilians, especially on the 28th of March, 1999, in the village of Mamusa. In the conversation with a larger group, I stayed for longer than an hour. If necessary, I could provide details.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your information, did any soldier from your unit steal something or commit any other crime?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In this counter-terrorist action not a single soldier under my command committed any crime, including theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any perpetrators of the crime of theft or any other crime in your unit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were perpetrators of crimes of theft, but I have to say that that was done exclusively outside of combat activities. Naturally, for all crimes uncovered we prosecuted them. You asked me about other crimes, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there any murders?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm interested now in the 27th and 28th of April, 1999. Who gave you the order for your activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, on the 27th and 28th of April some of the units were sent pursuant to the order of the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, at the time it was Colonel Veroljub Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, witness for the Prosecution Merita Deda said that in the village of Korenica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Cepic, we couldn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 27th of April, 6.00 in the morning, the village of Korenica, did your forces enter that village and did they wear hats?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th in the morning at 6.00, part of my unit was located at the blockade going all the way down to the river, which means that they were not in the village of Korenica. As for the other question, my soldiers never wore hats, nor does such piece of uniform exist in the Army of Yugoslavia at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, Martin Pnishi Prosecution witness, claims that he saw members of the army with their rank insignia on their shoulders [Realtime transcript read in error "soldiers"]. Did the members of the Army of Yugoslavia have their rank insignia on their shoulders and were they located in the village of Meja, as this witness stated?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an error in transcript, page 75, line 24, the word is rank insignia on their soldiers, not soldiers but shoulders. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, just a small correction. Would you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My all means. My soldiers were not in Meja village. VJ officers have no ranks displayed on their shoulder straps, on the shoulder strap of their combat uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may I continue, Your Honour? May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, were there any attacks against your forces from the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On an almost daily basis the Defence sector of my battalion was subjected to attacks from the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What sort of attacks were those?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part those were combined attacks, NATO air-strikes, NATO strikes, primarily air-strikes; attacks by Siptar terrorist forces, ground attacks; normally there would be artillery support by some parts of the armed forces of Albania. I can share a lot of detail if you have time or need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the intensity of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The intensity was high, and as the war continued it kept increasing. The last day NATO used strategic fighter planes, B-52, to attack my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any civilian groups moving about throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly noticed civilian groups moving about during the war. It wasn't something that was happening all the time, I have to say. Most of this occurred at the beginning of the war, but it also was known to happen during the remainder of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: According to your information, what caused this and was it just one ethnic group that was moving about?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't just one ethnic group. Siptars were leaving the area, Serbs were leaving the area, gypsies were leaving the area, everyone was leaving the area. There was a daily campaign, especially in the early days of the war, to intimidate civilians, and this campaign was being conducted by NATO and their air force. You asked me about the causes of this. There were people who were leaving their homes. I spoke to some of those people. When prompted about the main reason for leaving, they invariably mentioned their fear of NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is not difficult to notice that you have some trouble walking and speaking. What is this a consequence of?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. This is a consequence of the fact that I took ill during the war back in 1999. That's when the illness struck.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do we know what caused this illness?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There are assumptions about the cause, and unfortunately no more than assumptions. Because doctors tend to not look into the causes, they just treat the consequences. The most recent theory is that I was poisoned by some harmful substance and that this caused some damage to my central nervous system. This is the result, and the result is there for all to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your war diary under the heading "telegrams," we see in relation to the 30th of May, 1999, a reference to a volunteer platoon known as the Phantom Platoon. Can you explain what this is about, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. After the ground forces launched their attack across the Pastrik, Mount Pastrik, NATO referred to this as Strela Dva, Operation Arrow 2. For the first couple of days the forces managed to take a number of elevations along the ridge, thereby exposing the left flank of my unit. This was the reason that I ordered the commander of the 1st Company, and those were the men organizing our defence in that area, to take the elevations. For this purpose I told him to set up a platoon and to use soldiers, men, who volunteered to be involved in this exceptionally dangerous and complex mission, which of course he did. As far as I can remember, the commander of that platoon was Lieutenant-Colonel Kulundzic Jovica, or rather, second lieutenant, Kulundzic Jovica. There were men in that platoon who were military conscripts and those who were caught up in the term of their regular military term. You asked me about the name, the phantoms. This is based on the call-sign set up by that platoon commander when someone was trying to get in touch with them through radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were any members of that platoon killed?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that was the case. Rade Vejin from Zapotin [phoen] was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This soldier who was killed, Mr. Vejin, what was his status?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Rade Vejin was in the middle of his regular military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, how many of your soldiers were killed during the war and how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, seven of my soldiers were killed and 40 were wounded. Both among those killed and among those wounded there were a number of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement you describe something that you describe as a platoon that was meant to protect and take care of civilians. Just briefly, give me an example, if you can, of the sort of assistance that they provided.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to be brief if you're trying to describe something that happened, but I'll do my best. I think this was sometime in the second half of April 1999. We had just learned that the people who were living in the village of Jahovac were preparing to leave their village en masse and go to Albania. I dispatched the platoon's commander who went there who spoke to the locals and eventually led some of them to change their minds. As a result, they stayed for the duration of the war; that is, until such time as we withdrew from the Djakovica sector. I don't know what happened later, but there were many examples like that. So if you have more time I can furnish more examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, good afternoon, sir. My name is Dan Ivetic, and although your statement is rather extensive [Realtime transcript read in error "sensitive"] I apologise, but I do have to clear up a few items with you, as counsel for Sreten Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think your expression was extensive, is that correct, if you look at line 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I said extensive, I see that the line 9 has sensitive, so I stand corrected if I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said extensive. It's just to make sure it doesn't remain in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I would like to start first with the anti-terrorist action Reka. At paragraph 64 of your statement relative to this action you discuss how you received your orders from Colonel Zivkovic. Do you recall what other units or commanders received their orders from the Chief of Staff, Colonel Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, that is not how I refer to that anti-terrorist action. I don't call it Reka. As far as I know, that wasn't what it was called, although I don't know that it actually had a specific name. As for your question, one thing that I know for sure is that in Cabrat there were components of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade that were involved in blocking the area, specifically the anti-aircraft defence element; and as far as I can remember also some from the 125th Motorised Brigade. They were my right-hand neighbour. There were some men from that battalion, but I really can't be any more specific as to how strong. I know that they were in the general area of Smonica village and Nivokaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you referred to that as paragraph 64. That is not the paragraph 64 I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I had been alerted of that earlier that I think some of the paragraphs I have are not the same. I've made corrections in the remainder of my questions, but I see this one still has the original number. I will have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are the first words of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll have to find my version to -- let's see. One moment. 68, I believe, is where he talks about receiving the task from the Chief of Staff, Colonel Veroljub Zinkovic in the English but Zivkovic in the Serbian, so I believe 68 is what I have for that paragraph in the hard copy that I have before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if we could take a few moments. You've mentioned the assignments of both yourself and some of the neighbouring forces. I would like to call up IC172, an exhibit that has been previously created by another VJ participant in this anti-terrorist action which -- as you say did not have a specific name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While that's coming up could I ask you just to clarify one thing for me. The task, the issuing of the task by Zivkovic for this action, was that given to you orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it normal for the Chief of Staff to issue orders to the commander of a combat group orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't give you an answer to that question because I did not normally receive orders from him. As far as I can remember now, from the forward command post where -- in Djakovica where the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps was, I received only twice an order directly. And in relation to this, in the telephone conversation by brigade commander ordered me to call saying that something needed to be done, he wasn't quite sure what himself, and then I made a call and was given a very brief task, orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have in front of us IC172, which is a map of the Caragoj or Reka region that has been marked by a prior witness with respect to the forces that were engaged in frisking the terrain. If you could, sir, please, with the help of the usher, using any colour that -- that -- that you really deem appropriate identify -- draw and identify the blockade positions that your units had during this action. And if you require any, um, any assistance, I believe your combat report P2019 describes this as the Korenica TT 360 Groblje-Raskrsnica Puteva-Meja Orize-Kodra Kikes axis.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Black and red, all right. I suppose this is Djakovica. I can't see this -- I can't see the entire map, especially Cabrat. There is a trig called Kodra Kikes as you said, and there was a military police platoon there. This is bad here, this line here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take it by that you mean we can disregard the part of the line that goes off the screen and just consider the small line?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let the record reflect that the ...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly this is what it was because one can't see the entire map. I suppose that this here in the middle of the right side is the city of Djakovica. Perhaps I put it a bit lower, perhaps it's a bit more to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm just waiting for the transcript and translation to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that the black non-solid line just below Korenica and by Duznje is the line that the witness has now drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you now be in a position to also draw in, perhaps in another colour, the positions held by the 125th Motorised Brigade and mark the same with the number 125 as well as the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade of the PVO, marking that -- marking those positions and then identifying them with the number 52nd?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you of a limitation --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, the witness just said that he could only suppose, so it could be concluded that he cannot provide relevant information about units that were not under his command. That's precisely what the witness said, so any attempt to draw in positions of other units would be imprecise and unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can we establish a foundation for you asking the witness to do this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe when I asked him earlier he said he -- although he didn't know the numerical strength of the units involved, that he did know where they were located, one being on his right neighbouring side and the other one being on Cabrat. I could perhaps assist -- to at least have some reference point by identifying what General Zivanovic and Colonel Kotur said about where their units were located and see if the witness can recall -- if that coincides with the witness's recollection of where his neighbouring blockade forces were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave I regret that on page 83, line 22, not entire answer of the witness was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's enough information at 80, line 22, to 81, line 4 to show a foundation for asking him this, so please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Take them one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't we focus on the 52nd Artillery Rocket PVO Brigade that you had mentioned being in the region of Cabrat. The -- Colonel Kotur I believe said it was on a ridge between Osek Hilja and the old part of Djakovica town. Does that comport with your recollection of where this neighbouring blockade force was situated for purposes of this action?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part I said that the Cabrat hill, it's not indicated here, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If you could use, I guess, red or some other colour to differentiate from the black lines that you have drawn to depict your own axis of blockade.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you put a 5-2 near those two disjointed lines that you have drawn in near Osek Hilja on the map.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, with respect to your other neighbouring blockade force, the elements of the 125th Motorised Brigade, I believe in his testimony here General Zivanovic said that one company was at the Smonica-Stubla point or axes, and that one volunteer company was at the Berijac Nivokaz. Does that comport with your recollection of the location, if not in numerical strength of in neighbouring blockade force?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not consistent with my knowledge from that period of time. I said that they could have been there. I knew what their area of defence was, but if this is what General Zivanovic says I have no reason to doubt his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's approach it this way. Can you draw in, again using the red pen, the placement and location of the blockade line as you recall it of the 125th -- elements of the 125th Motorised Brigade for purposes of this action that was undertaken on the 27th and 28th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I said that I supposed and that most likely they were in the sector of Smonica village, that's the sector here, Nivokaz, but to draw it in with precision I would have to know which forces those were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I apologise, I had to wait for the translation and the transcript. If you could please mark that one solid line that you have drawn to the left of Smonica, if you could mark that with a 125 to signify the particular unit issued.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if we can have this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem with that is it's nowhere near Nivokaz on this map, but perhaps you could try and clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you in a position to identify the axis Berijac-Nivokaz that I understand --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to draw a line --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you are in a position to do so, yes, to identify the line of blockade that you believe the units of the 125th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's done that surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I drew a line. You asked me to draw a line showing the axis. I connected Nivokaz, Beljak, Stubla, Smonica, that's the axis. I didn't say that that was the line of the blockade because I have no knowledge concerning that particular unit. You asked to show the axis, and I apologise that it's not quite straight. In the military it's better to make it straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the position is that the small red line left of Smonica is the location of the 125th according to the best information the witness can give us, and the two red lines running from just to the right of that Nivokaz are immaterial for this exercise. Please continue -- well, sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for completing this. What I'd like to highlight is that General Zivanovic tried to draw it here in the courtroom and that wasn't admitted in the evidence, and what colonel is drawing in now, at least in my mind, does not correspond to the words of General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nor has he intended that the drawing should. What the witness is giving us is his best information, but he's also told you that quite separately he has no reason to doubt what Zivanovic said. So we have different information from two witnesses that we will have to make the most of in due course. Please continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could save this as an IC number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's been done yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC174, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Given the Prosecution's warnings, I have three questions I believe I ought to do in private session to protect identities of the Prosecution witnesses. I don't know if these are the witnesses that the prosecution is referring to, but I would rather err on the side of caution and I should be able to finish the questions in the time that we have left in this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vukovic, we have to conclude our proceedings for the day at this stage. That means you need to return tomorrow to continue with your evidence; that will be at 2.00 -- sorry, 2.15 tomorrow afternoon in this courtroom. It is extremely important that between now and then you have no discussion with anyone at all about the evidence in this case. You can discuss other subjects, but with no person whatsoever must you touch on any aspect of the evidence in the case. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
